Senior colleagues dismiss Bragg’s migration figures as ‘personal views’ while others say critical response is an ‘overreaction’ Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast Liberal senator Andrew McLachlan has publicly backed Andrew Bragg and urged colleagues to “follow his lead” after a public speech that has split colleagues and triggered a rebuke from opposition leader, Angus Taylor. At the National Press Club on Wednesday, Bragg announced a policy to slash the national construction code and suggested net overseas migration should be dropped from the current level of about 300,000 to below 180,000 a year to keep pace with new housing builds.

Senior colleagues, including Taylor, were quick to dismiss the migration figure this week, saying they were Bragg’s “personal views” and that the party’s policy was yet to be finalised. The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson had said: “I don’t think you should bank that at all” in response to the number. Privately, Taylor counselled his frontbencher. Moderates, including McLachlan and Queensland senator Paul Scarr, called Bragg’s speech “terrific” while others privately said the reaction by the media and some internally was “overblown”. McLachlan, an outspoken South Australian senator who has publicly criticised his party’s positions on migration and the climate crisis, said Bragg “delivered a masterclass in thought leadership”. “His address was an important step in the development of a policy suite that seeks advance the nation,” McLachlan told Guardian Australia.

“His aspiration for Australia is admirable. Every member of the Coalition should follow his lead and discuss policy pathways openly.” Scarr, who has also defied his party and crossed the Senate floor in March to censure Pauline Hanson after she wore a burqa in the Upper House, said he “thought it was a terrific speech. High-level and reinforcing our core Liberal values”. Other Liberals have been frustrated at the intervention by Bragg, with one MP saying privately colleagues were angry at the lack of discipline and this could be “his last chance”. Even after critical commentary from his colleagues in recent days, Bragg has maintained it was important to talk about big ideas.

Senior colleagues dismiss Bragg’s migration figures as ‘personal views’ while others say critical response is an ‘overreaction’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Liberal senator Andrew McLachlan has publicly backed Andrew Bragg and urged colleagues to “follow his lead” after a public speech that has split colleagues and triggered a rebuke from opposition leader, Angus Taylor.

At the National Press Club on Wednesday, Bragg announced a policy to slash the national construction code and suggested net overseas migration should be dropped from the current level of about 300,000 to below 180,000 a year to keep pace with new housing builds.

Senior colleagues, including Taylor, were quick to dismiss the migration figure this week, saying they were Bragg’s “personal views” and that the party’s policy was yet to be finalised. The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson had said: “I don’t think you should bank that at all” in response to the number.

Privately, Taylor counselled his frontbencher.

Moderates, including McLachlan and Queensland senator Paul Scarr, called Bragg’s speech “terrific” while others privately said the reaction by the media and some internally was “overblown”.

McLachlan, an outspoken South Australian senator who has publicly criticised his party’s positions on migration and the climate crisis, said Bragg “delivered a masterclass in thought leadership”.

“His address was an important step in the development of a policy suite that seeks advance the nation,” McLachlan told Guardian Australia.

“His aspiration for Australia is admirable. Every member of the Coalition should follow his lead and discuss policy pathways openly.”

Scarr, who has also defied his party and crossed the Senate floor in March to censure Pauline Hanson after she wore a burqa in the Upper House, said he “thought it was a terrific speech. High-level and reinforcing our core Liberal values”.

Other Liberals have been frustrated at the intervention by Bragg, with one MP saying privately colleagues were angry at the lack of discipline and this could be “his last chance”.

Even after critical commentary from his colleagues in recent days, Bragg has maintained it was important to talk about big ideas.

The NSW senator said while many of his ideas, such as a specific net overseas migration target, hadn’t been green-ticked by the shadow cabinet, it was important to “move the debate on”.
